claim: The CEPH/Utah dataset comprises 33 three-generation families.
source: The CEPH/Utah dataset comprises 33 three-generation families.
evidence: Stated in the abstract and shown in Figure 1a caption.

claim: 603 individuals from 33, three-generation CEPH/Utah pedigrees were sequenced to a genome-wide median depth of ~30X.
source: We sequenced the genomes of 603 individuals from 33, three-generation CEPH/Utah pedigrees to a genome-wide median depth of ~30X (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1)
evidence: Direct statement of sequencing methodology and depth.

claim: 10 samples were removed from further analysis following quality control using peddy.
source: We sequenced the genomes of 603 individuals from 33, three-generation CEPH/Utah pedigrees to a genome-wide median depth of ~30X (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1), and removed 10 samples from further analysis following quality control using peddy (Pedersen and Quinlan, 2017a).
evidence: Direct statement of sample removal after quality control.

claim: A total of 4,671 germline de novo mutations were identified in 70 second-generation individuals.
source: After standard quality filtering, we identified a total of 4,671 germline de novo mutations in 70 second-generation individuals, each of which was transmitted to at least one offspring in the third generation (Figure 1a, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Direct statement of DNM count in second generation.

claim: Approximately 92% (4,298 of 4,671) of DNMs observed in the second generation were single nucleotide variants (SNVs).
source: Approximately 92% (4,298 of 4,671) of DNMs observed in the second generation were single nucleotide variants (SNVs), and the remainder were small (<=10 bp) insertion/deletion variants.

claim: The false positive rate for de novo mutation detection strategy is 4.5%.
source: The eight parents of four second-generation samples were re-sequenced to a median depth of ~60X (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d), allowing us to estimate a false positive rate of 4.5% for our de novo mutation detection strategy (Materials and methods).
evidence: Estimated from re-sequencing data at higher depth.

claim: The median germline mutation rate for SNVs is 1.10 x 10-8 per base pair per generation.
source: Taking all second-generation samples together, we calculated median germline mutation rates of 1.10 x 10-8 and 9.29 x 10-10 per base pair per generation for SNVs and indels, respectively, which corroborate prior estimates based on family genome sequencing with roughly comparable parental ages (Jónsson et al., 2017; Kong et al., 2012; Besenbacher et al., 2016; Rahbari et al., 2016).
evidence: Calculated from observed DNMs and callable genome fraction.

claim: The median germline mutation rate for indels is 9.29 x 10-10 per base pair per generation.
source: Taking all second-generation samples together, we calculated median germline mutation rates of 1.10 x 10-8 and 9.29 x 10-10 per base pair per generation for SNVs and indels, respectively, which corroborate prior estimates based on family genome sequencing with roughly comparable parental ages (Jónsson et al., 2017; Kong et al., 2012; Besenbacher et al., 2016; Rahbari et al., 2016).
evidence: Calculated from observed DNMs and callable genome fraction.

claim: The average number of de novo SNVs per genome is 70.1 at average paternal and maternal ages of 29.1 and 26.0 years, respectively.
source: Extrapolating to a diploid genome size of ~6.4 Gbp, we therefore estimate an average number of 70.1 de novo SNVs and 5.9 de novo indels per genome, at average paternal and maternal ages of 29.1 and 26.0 years, respectively (Sasani, 2019).
evidence: Extrapolated from mutation rate and genome size.

claim: The average number of de novo indels per genome is 5.9 at average paternal and maternal ages of 29.1 and 26.0 years, respectively.
source: Extrapolating to a diploid genome size of ~6.4 Gbp, we therefore estimate an average number of 70.1 de novo SNVs and 5.9 de novo indels per genome, at average paternal and maternal ages of 29.1 and 26.0 years, respectively (Sasani, 2019).
evidence: Extrapolated from mutation rate and genome size.

claim: The parental gamete-of-origin was determined for a median of 98.5% of de novo variants per second-generation individual (range: 90.3–100%).
source: We determined the parental gamete-of-origin for a median of 98.5% of de novo variants per second-generation individual (range: 90.3–100%) by leveraging haplotype sharing across all three generations in a family (Kong et al., 2012; Jónsson et al., 2017), as well as read tracing of DNMs to informative sites in the parents (Figure 1b, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Determined using haplotype sharing and read tracing methods.

claim: The ratio of paternal to maternal DNMs was 3.96:1.
source: The ratio of paternal to maternal DNMs was 3.96:1, and 79.8% of DNMs were paternal in origin.

claim: 79.8% of DNMs were paternal in origin.
source: The ratio of paternal to maternal DNMs was 3.96:1, and 79.8% of DNMs were paternal in origin.

claim: There is a significant paternal age effect of 1.44 (95% CI: 1.12–1.77, p<2e-16) additional DNMs per year.
source: After fitting Poisson regressions, we observed a significant paternal age effect of 1.44 (95% CI: 1.12–1.77, p<2e-16) additional DNMs per year, and a significant maternal age effect of 0.38 (95% CI: 0.21–0.55, p=1.24e-5) DNMs per year (Figure 2a).

claim: There is a significant maternal age effect of 0.38 (95% CI: 0.21–0.55, p=1.24e-5) DNMs per year.
source: After fitting Poisson regressions, we observed a significant paternal age effect of 1.44 (95% CI: 1.12–1.77, p<2e-16) additional DNMs per year, and a significant maternal age effect of 0.38 (95% CI: 0.21–0.55, p=1.24e-5) DNMs per year (Figure 2a).

claim: In maternal mutations, there was an enrichment of C > T transitions in a non-CpG context (p=7.65e-6).
source: In maternal mutations, there was an enrichment of C > T transitions in a non-CpG context (p=7.65e-6, Chi-squared test of independence), and we observed an enrichment of T > G transversions in paternal mutations (p=4.93e-3, Chi-squared test of independence).
evidence: Determined by Chi-squared test comparing mutation spectra.

claim: There was an enrichment of T > G transversions in paternal mutations (p=4.93e-3).
source: In maternal mutations, there was an enrichment of C > T transitions in a non-CpG context (p=7.65e-6, Chi-squared test of independence), and we observed an enrichment of T > G transversions in paternal mutations (p=4.93e-3, Chi-squared test of independence).
evidence: Determined by Chi-squared test comparing mutation spectra.

claim: Maternal and paternal enrichments of C > T and T > G, respectively, have been reported in recent studies of de novo mutation spectra.
source: Maternal and paternal enrichments of C > T and T > G, respectively, have been reported in recent studies of de novo mutation spectra, though the mechanisms underlying these observations are currently unclear (Goldmann et al., 2016; Jónsson et al., 2017).

claim: No significant differences were found in the mutational spectra of children born to older or younger parents.
source: We additionally stratified second-generation individuals by the ages of their parents at birth and found no significant differences in the mutational spectra of children born to older or younger parents, though we may be underpowered to detect these differences in our dataset (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Statistical comparison of mutation spectra by parental age groups.

claim: 24,975 de novo SNVs and small indels were detected in 350 individuals in the third generation.
source: In total, we detected 24,975 de novo SNVs and small indels in 350 individuals in the third generation (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Direct count of DNMs in third generation.

claim: A parental gamete-of-origin was confidently determined for 5,336 (median of 21% per third-generation individual; range of 8–38%) third-generation DNMs using read tracing.
source: Of these, we were able to confidently determine a parental gamete-of-origin for 5,336 (median of 21% per third-generation individual; range of 8–38%) using read tracing, and assign 4,201 (78.7%) of these to fathers.

claim: 4,201 (78.7%) of phased third-generation DNMs were assigned to fathers.
source: Of these, we were able to confidently determine a parental gamete-of-origin for 5,336 (median of 21% per third-generation individual; range of 8–38%) using read tracing, and assign 4,201 (78.7%) of these to fathers.

claim: Taking all third-generation individuals into account, the slope of the paternal age effect is estimated to be 1.72 DNMs per year (95% CI: 1.58–1.85, p<2e-16).
source: Taking all third-generation individuals into account, we estimate the slope of the paternal age effect to be 1.72 DNMs per year (95% CI: 1.58–1.85, p<2e-16).

claim: The effect of paternal age on offspring DNM counts varied widely across pedigrees, from only 0.19 (95% CI: −1.05–1.44) to nearly 3.24 (95% CI: 2.24–4.24) additional DNMs per year.
source: Overall, the effect of paternal age on offspring DNM counts varied widely across pedigrees, from only 0.19 (95% CI: −1.05–1.44) to nearly 3.24 (95% CI: 2.24–4.24) additional DNMs per year.

claim: A goodness-of-fit test supported the use of a 'family-aware' regression model when compared to a model that ignores family membership (ANOVA: p=9.36e-10).
source: A goodness-of-fit test supported the use of a 'family-aware' regression model when compared to a model that ignores family membership, even after accounting for variable sequencing coverage across third-generation samples (median autosomal base pairs covered = 2,582,875,060; ANOVA: p=9.36e-10).

claim: The interaction between paternal age and family membership improved the fit of the linear model (p=0.043).
source: Moreover, we found that the interaction between paternal age and family membership improved the fit of the linear model (p=0.043, Appendix 1—table 1), suggesting that inter-family variability involves differences in paternal age effects (i.e., the slopes of each regression).
evidence: ANOVA test of model with interaction term.

claim: 720 single-nucleotide germline mosaic mutations were identified at a total of 303 unique sites.
source: In total, we identified 720 single-nucleotide germline mosaic mutations at a total of 303 unique sites, which were subsequently corroborated through visual inspection using the Integrative Genomics Viewer (IGV) (Supplementary file 4) (Thorvaldsdóttir et al., 2013).
evidence: Direct count of mosaic mutations validated by visual inspection.

claim: Of the phased shared germline mosaic mutations, 124/260 (47.7%) were paternal in origin.
source: Of the phased shared germline mosaic mutations, 124/260 (47.7%) were paternal in origin; thus, the mutations that occurred following PGCS likely occurred irrespective of any parental sex biases on mutation counts.

claim: Approximately 3.1% (720/23,399) of all single-nucleotide DNMs observed in the third generation likely arose during or following PGCS in a parent's germline.
source: Overall, approximately 3.1% (720/23,399) of all single-nucleotide DNMs observed in the third generation likely arose during or following PGCS in a parent's germline, confirming that these variants comprise a non-negligible fraction of all de novo germline mutations.
evidence: Calculated from counts of mosaic and total DNMs.

claim: The mutation spectrum for non-shared germline de novo variants was significantly different than the spectrum for shared germline mosaic variants.
source: The mutation spectrum for non-shared germline de novo variants was significantly different than the spectrum for shared germline mosaic variants (Figure 4b).
evidence: Statistical comparison of mutation spectra shown in Figure 4b.

claim: There were enrichments of CpG >TpG and C > A mutations in shared germline mosaic variants when compared to all unshared germline de novo variants observed in the third generation.
source: Specifically, we found enrichments of CpG >TpG and C > A mutations, and a depletion of T > C mutations, in shared germline mosaic variants when compared to all unshared germline de novo variants observed in the third generation (Figure 4b).

claim: There was a depletion of T > C mutations in shared germline mosaic variants when compared to all unshared germline de novo variants observed in the third generation.
source: Specifically, we found enrichments of CpG >TpG and C > A mutations, and a depletion of T > C mutations, in shared germline mosaic variants when compared to all unshared germline de novo variants observed in the third generation (Figure 4b).

claim: An enrichment of CpG >TpG mutations in germline mosaic DNMs was also seen in a recent report on mutations shared between siblings.
source: An enrichment of CpG >TpG mutations in germline mosaic DNMs, which was also seen in a recent report on mutations shared between siblings (Jónsson et al., 2018), is particularly intriguing, as many C > T transitions in a CG dinucleotide context are thought to occur due to spontaneous deamination of methylated cytosine (Fryxell and Zuckerkandl, 2000).

claim: Many C > T transitions in a CG dinucleotide context are thought to occur due to spontaneous deamination of methylated cytosine.
source: An enrichment of CpG >TpG mutations in germline mosaic DNMs, which was also seen in a recent report on mutations shared between siblings (Jónsson et al., 2018), is particularly intriguing, as many C > T transitions in a CG dinucleotide context are thought to occur due to spontaneous deamination of methylated cytosine (Fryxell and Zuckerkandl, 2000).

claim: DNA methylation patterns are highly dynamic during gametogenesis.
source: Indeed, DNA methylation patterns are highly dynamic during gametogenesis; evidence in mouse demonstrates that the early primordial germ cells are highly methylated, but experience a global loss of methylation during expansion and migration to the genital ridge, followed by a re-establishment of epigenetic marks (at different time points in males and females) (Seisenberger et al., 2012; Reik et al., 2001).
evidence: Referenced from prior publications on mouse gametogenesis.

claim: The number of shared germline mosaic DNMs does not increase with paternal age (p=0.647).
source: As reported in the recent analysis of germline mosaicism (Jónsson et al., 2018), we observed that the number of shared germline mosaic DNMs does not increase with paternal age (p=0.647, Figure 4c, Materials and methods).

claim: A significant age-related decrease in the proportion of shared germline mosaic DNMs was observed (p=1.61e-5).
source: Consistent with this expectation, we observed a significant age-related decrease in the proportion of shared germline mosaic DNMs (p=1.61e-5, Figure 4e).

claim: Neither the mosaic fraction nor the number of mosaic DNMs observed in third-generation children are significantly associated with the number of siblings in a family.
source: Although families with large numbers of siblings are expected to offer greater power to detect shared, germline mosaic DNMs, we verified that neither the mosaic fraction nor the number of mosaic DNMs observed in third-generation children are significantly associated with the number of siblings in a family (Materials and methods).
evidence: Statistical analysis described in Materials and methods.

claim: 475 putative autosomal gonosomal DNMs were identified.
source: In total, we identified 475 putative autosomal gonosomal DNMs, which were also validated by visual inspection (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: Direct count of gonosomal DNMs validated by visual inspection.

claim: 52% (249/475) of all gonosomal DNMs occurred on a paternal haplotype.
source: In contrast to single-gamete germline DNMs observed in the second-generation, gonosomal mutations appeared to be sex-balanced with respect to the parental haplotype on which they occurred; 52% (249/475) of all gonosomal DNMs occurred on a paternal haplotype, as compared to ~80% of germline DNMs observed in the second generation.

claim: No significant enrichment of particular gonosomal mutation types was observed on either parental haplotype at a false discovery rate of 0.05.
source: Similarly, no significant enrichment of particular gonosomal mutation types was observed on either parental haplotype at a false discovery rate of 0.05 (Figure 5b), though we found that T > A transversions are enriched in gonosomal DNMs when compared to single-gamete germline DNMs observed in the second generation (p=2.32e-3) (Figure 5c).

claim: T > A transversions are enriched in gonosomal DNMs when compared to single-gamete germline DNMs observed in the second generation (p=2.32e-3).
source: Similarly, no significant enrichment of particular gonosomal mutation types was observed on either parental haplotype at a false discovery rate of 0.05 (Figure 5b), though we found that T > A transversions are enriched in gonosomal DNMs when compared to single-gamete germline DNMs observed in the second generation (p=2.32e-3) (Figure 5c).

claim: There were no significant effects of parental age on gonosomal DNM counts (maternal age, p=0.132; paternal age, p=0.225).
source: Unlike single-gamete germline DNMs, there were no significant effects of parental age on gonosomal DNM counts (maternal age, p=0.132; paternal age, p=0.225) (Figure 5d).

claim: Over 9% (475/5,017) of all candidate autosomal germline mutations observed in the second generation were post-zygotic in these second-generation individuals.
source: Overall, our results demonstrate that over 9% (475/5,017) of all candidate autosomal germline mutations observed in the second generation were, in fact, post-zygotic in these second-generation individuals.
evidence: Calculated from counts of gonosomal and total candidate DNMs.

claim: Approximately 6% of candidate de novo mutations detected in the second generation with an allele balance >= 0.2 (303/5,017) were determined to be post-zygotic, and present in both somatic and germ cells.
source: Perhaps most importantly, approximately 6% of candidate de novo mutations detected in the second generation with an allele balance >= 0.2 (303/5,017) were determined to be post-zygotic, and present in both somatic and germ cells.
evidence: Calculated from counts of gonosomal DNMs meeting allele balance threshold.

claim: The CEPH/Utah pedigrees have considerably more (min = 4, max = 16, median = 8) offspring than those used in many prior studies of the human mutation rate.
source: The CEPH/Utah pedigrees are uniquely powerful for the study of germline mutation dynamics in that they have considerably more (min = 4, max = 16, median = 8) offspring than those used in many prior studies of the human mutation rate (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Direct statement of offspring counts in the dataset.

claim: Multiple offspring birth dates span up to 27 years in the CEPH/Utah pedigrees.
source: Multiple offspring, whose birth dates span up to 27 years, motivated our investigation of parental age effects on DNM counts within families and allowed us to ask whether these effects differed across families.
evidence: Direct statement of birth date span.

claim: The structure of all CEPH/Utah pedigrees enables the use of haplotype sharing through three generations to determine the parental haplotype of origin for nearly all DNMs in the second generation.
source: The structure of all CEPH/Utah pedigrees (Supplementary file 1) also enables the use of haplotype sharing through three generations to determine the parental haplotype of origin for nearly all DNMs in the second generation.
evidence: Description of phasing methodology enabled by pedigree structure.

claim: The CEPH/Utah families have played a central role in our understanding of human genetic variation.
source: The CEPH/Utah families have played a central role in our understanding of human genetic variation (Prescott et al., 2008; 1000 Genomes Project Consortium et al., 2015) by guiding the construction of reference linkage maps for the Human Genome Project (Lander et al., 2001), defining haplotypes in the International HapMap Project (International HapMap Consortium, 2003), and characterizing genome-wide variation in the 1000 Genomes Project (1000 Genomes Project Consortium et al., 2015).

claim: The CEPH/Utah families guided the construction of reference linkage maps for the Human Genome Project.
source: The CEPH/Utah families have played a central role in our understanding of human genetic variation (Prescott et al., 2008; 1000 Genomes Project Consortium et al., 2015) by guiding the construction of reference linkage maps for the Human Genome Project (Lander et al., 2001), defining haplotypes in the International HapMap Project (International HapMap Consortium, 2003), and characterizing genome-wide variation in the 1000 Genomes Project (1000 Genomes Project Consortium et al., 2015).

claim: The CEPH/Utah families defined haplotypes in the International HapMap Project.
source: The CEPH/Utah families have played a central role in our understanding of human genetic variation (Prescott et al., 2008; 1000 Genomes Project Consortium et al., 2015) by guiding the construction of reference linkage maps for the Human Genome Project (Lander et al., 2001), defining haplotypes in the International HapMap Project (International HapMap Consortium, 2003), and characterizing genome-wide variation in the 1000 Genomes Project (1000 Genomes Project Consortium et al., 2015).

claim: The CEPH/Utah families characterized genome-wide variation in the 1000 Genomes Project.
source: The CEPH/Utah families have played a central role in our understanding of human genetic variation (Prescott et al., 2008; 1000 Genomes Project Consortium et al., 2015) by guiding the construction of reference linkage maps for the Human Genome Project (Lander et al., 2001), defining haplotypes in the International HapMap Project (International HapMap Consortium, 2003), and characterizing genome-wide variation in the 1000 Genomes Project (1000 Genomes Project Consortium et al., 2015).

claim: DNMs are an important source of genetic disease.
source: As DNMs are an important source of genetic disease (Campbell et al., 2014b; Campbell et al., 2015; Biesecker and Spinner, 2013; Forsberg et al., 2017; Acuna-Hidalgo et al., 2016; Veltman and Brunner, 2012), it is critical to understand the rates of mosaic DNM transmission in families.

claim: Whole genome sequencing of pedigrees has enabled direct estimates of the human germline mutation rate by identifying mutations present in offspring yet absent from their parents.
source: In the last decade, whole genome sequencing of pedigrees has enabled direct estimates of the human germline mutation rate by identifying mutations present in offspring yet absent from their parents (de novo mutations, DNMs) (Ségurel et al., 2014; Scally and Durbin, 2012; Jónsson et al., 2017; Goldmann et al., 2016; Kong et al., 2012; Roach et al., 2010; Francioli et al., 2015).

claim: Pedigree-based studies have produced mutation rate estimates nearly two-fold lower than those from phylogenetic comparison.
source: Numerous studies have employed this approach to analyze the mutation rate in cohorts of small, nuclear families, producing estimates nearly two-fold lower than those from phylogenetic comparison (Roach et al., 2010; Kong et al., 2012; Jónsson et al., 2017; Goldmann et al., 2016; Scally and Durbin, 2012; Shendure and Akey, 2015; Turner et al., 2017).

claim: The number of DNMs increases with both maternal and paternal ages.
source: These studies have demonstrated that the number of DNMs increases with both maternal and paternal ages; such age effects can likely be attributed to a number of factors, including the increased mitotic divisions in sperm cells following puberty, an accumulation of damage-associated mutation, and substantial epigenetic reprogramming undergone by germ cells (Jónsson et al., 2017; Kong et al., 2012; Goldmann et al., 2016; Rahbari et al., 2016; Crow, 2000; Gao et al., 2019).

claim: Age effects on DNM counts can likely be attributed to increased mitotic divisions in sperm cells following puberty, an accumulation of damage-associated mutation, and substantial epigenetic reprogramming undergone by germ cells.
source: These studies have demonstrated that the number of DNMs increases with both maternal and paternal ages; such age effects can likely be attributed to a number of factors, including the increased mitotic divisions in sperm cells following puberty, an accumulation of damage-associated mutation, and substantial epigenetic reprogramming undergone by germ cells (Jónsson et al., 2017; Kong et al., 2012; Goldmann et al., 2016; Rahbari et al., 2016; Crow, 2000; Gao et al., 2019).

claim: There is evidence that the mutational spectra of de novo mutations differ in the male and female germlines.
source: There is also evidence that the mutational spectra of de novo mutations differ in the male and female germlines (Jónsson et al., 2017; Goldmann et al., 2016; Francioli et al., 2015; Gao et al., 2019; Agarwal and Przeworski, 2019).

claim: A recent study of three two-generation pedigrees indicated that paternal age effects may differ across families.
source: Furthermore, a recent study of three two-generation pedigrees, each with 4 or five children, indicated that paternal age effects may differ across families (Rahbari et al., 2016).

claim: Two-generation families with few offspring provide limited power to quantify parental age effects on mutation rates.
source: However, two-generation families with few offspring provide limited power to quantify parental age effects on mutation rates and restrict the ability to assign a gamete-of-origin to ~20–30% of DNMs (Rahbari et al., 2016; Jónsson et al., 2017; Goldmann et al., 2016).

claim: Two-generation families restrict the ability to assign a gamete-of-origin to ~20–30% of DNMs.
source: However, two-generation families with few offspring provide limited power to quantify parental age effects on mutation rates and restrict the ability to assign a gamete-of-origin to ~20–30% of DNMs (Rahbari et al., 2016; Jónsson et al., 2017; Goldmann et al., 2016).

claim: When compared to a multiple regression that includes the effects of both paternal and maternal age, a model that takes family membership into account remained a significantly better fit (ANOVA: p=2.12e-5).
source: Finally, when compared to a multiple regression that includes the effects of both paternal and maternal age, a model that takes family membership into account remained a significantly better fit (ANOVA: p=2.12e-5).

claim: The high degree of correlation between paternal and maternal ages makes it difficult to tease out the individual contributions of each parent to the observed inter-family differences.
source: The high degree of correlation between paternal and maternal ages makes it difficult to tease out the individual contributions of each parent to the observed inter-family differences.

claim: The results suggest the existence of substantial variability in parental age effects across CEPH/Utah families, which could involve both genetic and environmental factors that differ among families.
source: Nonetheless, these results suggest the existence of substantial variability in parental age effects across CEPH/Utah families, which could involve both genetic and environmental factors that differ among families.

claim: If a de novo variant arises during or after primordial germ cell specification (PGCS), that variant may be present in multiple resulting gametes and absent from somatic cells.
source: Generally, studies of de novo mutation focus on variants that arise in a single parental gamete. However, if a de novo variant arises during or after primordial germ cell specification (PGCS), that variant may be present in multiple resulting gametes and absent from somatic cells (Rahbari et al., 2016; Acuna-Hidalgo et al., 2015; Campbell et al., 2014b; Tang et al., 2016; Jónsson et al., 2018; Campbell et al., 2015; Biesecker and Spinner, 2013).

claim: Variants arising during or after PGCS can be present in more than one offspring as apparent de novo mutations.
source: Generally, studies of de novo mutation focus on variants that arise in a single parental gamete. However, if a de novo variant arises during or after primordial germ cell specification (PGCS), that variant may be present in multiple resulting gametes and absent from somatic cells (Rahbari et al., 2016; Acuna-Hidalgo et al., 2015; Campbell et al., 2014b; Tang et al., 2016; Jónsson et al., 2018; Campbell et al., 2015; Biesecker and Spinner, 2013). These variants can therefore be present in more than one offspring as apparent de novo mutations.

claim: The large number of third-generation siblings in each CEPH/Utah family provided substantially higher power to detect germline mosaicism that occurred in the second generation than in prior studies.
source: Given the large number of third-generation siblings in each CEPH/Utah family, we had substantially higher power to detect germline mosaicism that occurred in in the second generation than in prior studies.

claim: The mutations that occurred following PGCS likely occurred irrespective of any parental sex biases on mutation counts.
source: Of the phased shared germline mosaic mutations, 124/260 (47.7%) were paternal in origin; thus, the mutations that occurred following PGCS likely occurred irrespective of any parental sex biases on mutation counts.
evidence: Inference from approximately equal paternal and maternal fractions.

claim: The observation of germline mosaicism has broad implications for the study of human disease and estimates of recurrence risks within families.
source: Our observation of germline mosaicism, a result of de novo mutations that occur during or post-PGCS, has broad implications for the study of human disease and estimates of recurrence risks within families (Jónsson et al., 2018; Campbell et al., 2014b; Biesecker and Spinner, 2013; Forsberg et al., 2017; Krupp et al., 2017).

claim: If a de novo mutation is found to underlie a genetic disorder in a child, it is critical to understand the risk of mutation recurrence in future offspring.
source: If a de novo mutation is found to underlie a genetic disorder in a child, it is critical to understand the risk of mutation recurrence in future offspring.

claim: Approximately 3% of germline de novo mutations originated as a mosaic in the germ cells of a parent.
source: We estimate that ~3% of germline de novo mutations originated as a mosaic in the germ cells of a parent.
evidence: Calculated from observed mosaic DNM fraction.

claim: This result corroborates recent reports that a substantial fraction of all germline DNMs may be recurrent within a family.
source: This result corroborates recent reports (Rahbari et al., 2016; Jónsson et al., 2018) and demonstrates that a substantial fraction of all germline DNMs may be recurrent within a family.

claim: The mutation spectrum of shared germline mosaic DNMs is significantly different than the spectrum for single-gamete germline DNMs.
source: We also find that the mutation spectrum of shared germline mosaic DNMs is significantly different than the spectrum for single-gamete germline DNMs, raising the intriguing possibility that different mechanisms contribute to de novo mutation accumulation throughout the proliferation of primordial germ cells and later stages of gametogenesis.

claim: Different mechanisms may contribute to de novo mutation accumulation throughout the proliferation of primordial germ cells and later stages of gametogenesis.
source: We also find that the mutation spectrum of shared germline mosaic DNMs is significantly different than the spectrum for single-gamete germline DNMs, raising the intriguing possibility that different mechanisms contribute to de novo mutation accumulation throughout the proliferation of primordial germ cells and later stages of gametogenesis.
evidence: Inference from observed differences in mutation spectra.

claim: The substantial epigenetic reprogramming that occurs following primordial germ cell specification may predispose cells at particular developmental time points to certain classes of de novo mutations, such as C > T transitions at CpG dinucleotide sites.
source: For instance, the substantial epigenetic reprogramming that occurs following primordial germ cell specification may predispose cells at particular developmental time points to certain classes of de novo mutations, such as C > T transitions at CpG dinucleotide sites (Gao et al., 2019).

claim: Recurrent DNMs across siblings can manifest as a consequence of gonosomal mosaicism in parents.
source: Recurrent DNMs across siblings can also manifest as a consequence of gonosomal mosaicism in parents (Biesecker and Spinner, 2013; Jónsson et al., 2018).

claim: Gonosomal mutations are sex-balanced with respect to the parental haplotype on which they occurred.
source: Although it can be difficult to distinguish gonosomal mosaicism from both single-gamete germline de novo mutation and germline mosaicism, we have identified a set of putative gonosomal mosaic mutations that are sex-balanced with respect to the parental haplotype on which they occurred, and do not exhibit any detectable dependence on parental age at birth.

claim: Gonosomal mutations do not exhibit any detectable dependence on parental age at birth.
source: Although it can be difficult to distinguish gonosomal mosaicism from both single-gamete germline de novo mutation and germline mosaicism, we have identified a set of putative gonosomal mosaic mutations that are sex-balanced with respect to the parental haplotype on which they occurred, and do not exhibit any detectable dependence on parental age at birth.
evidence: Statistical analysis of gonosomal DNMs vs parental age.

claim: Both observations (sex-balance and age-independence) are expected if gonosomal mutations arise after zygote fertilization, rather than during the process of gametogenesis.
source: Both of these observations are expected if gonosomal mutations arise after zygote fertilization, rather than during the process of gametogenesis.

claim: Approximately 10% of candidate germline de novo mutations in the study were gonosomal mutations that occurred during the early cell divisions of the offspring, rather than in a single parental gamete.
source: Overall, we estimate that approximately 10% of candidate germline de novo mutations in our study were, in fact, gonosomal mutations that occurred during the early cell divisions of the offspring, rather than in a single parental gamete.
evidence: Calculated from observed gonosomal DNM fraction.

claim: Prior work in cattle has estimated the fraction of mosaic DNMs that occur during early cell divisions to be even higher than in humans.
source: Prior work in cattle has estimated the fraction of mosaic DNMs that occur during early cell divisions to be even higher, suggesting that these mosaic mutations make up a large fraction of DNMs that are reported to have occurred in a single parental gamete (Harland et al., 2017).

claim: The results underscore the power of large, multi-generational pedigrees for the study of de novo human mutation.
source: These results underscore the power of large, multi-generational pedigrees for the study of de novo human mutation and yield new insight into the mutation dynamics that exist due to factors such as parental age and sex, as well as family of origin.

claim: The mutation rate variability observed is very likely an underestimate of the full range of variability worldwide.
source: Given that we studied only 33 large pedigrees, the mutation rate variability we observe is very likely an underestimate of the full range of variability worldwide.

claim: The CEPH/Utah pedigrees comprise mostly healthy individuals who resided within a relatively narrow geographic area at the time of collection.
source: The fact that there were detectable differences in parental age effects between families is striking in light of the fact that the CEPH/Utah pedigrees comprise mostly healthy individuals, and that at the time of collection they resided within a relatively narrow geographic area (Malhotra et al., 2005; Dausset et al., 1990).

claim: The results likely understate the true extent of variability in mutation rates and age effects among families with diverse inherited risk for mutation accumulation, and who experience a wide range of exposures, diets, and other environmental factors.
source: We therefore suspect that our results understate the true extent of variability in mutation rates and age effects among families with diverse inherited risk for mutation accumulation, and who experience a wide range of exposures, diets, and other environmental factors.

claim: A recent report identified substantial differences in the mutation spectra of variants in populations of varied ancestries, suggesting that genetic modifiers of the mutation rate may exist in humans.
source: Supporting this hypothesis, a recent report identified substantial differences in the mutation spectra of variants in populations of varied ancestries, suggesting that genetic modifiers of the mutation rate may exist in humans, as well as possible differences in environmental exposures (Harris and Pritchard, 2017; Mathieson and Reich, 2017).

claim: Variability in the age at which parents enter puberty could explain some of the range of de novo mutation counts in firstborn children across families.
source: Another explanation (that we are unable to explore) for the range of de novo mutation counts in firstborn children across families is variability in the age at which parents enter puberty.

claim: A father entering puberty at an older age could result in less elapsed time between the start of spermatogenesis and the fertilization of his first child's embryo, leading to fewer accumulated mutations.
source: For example, a father entering puberty at an older age could result in less elapsed time between the start of spermatogenesis and the fertilization of his first child's embryo. Compared to another male parent of the same age, his sperm will have accumulated fewer mutations by the time of conception.

claim: Replication errors are unlikely to be the sole source of de novo germline mutations.
source: Moreover, we note that replication errors are unlikely to be the sole source of de novo germline mutations (Gao et al., 2019).

claim: The potential sources of inter-family variability in mutation rates remain mysterious.
source: Overall, the potential sources of inter-family variability in mutation rates remain mysterious, and we anticipate that future studies will be needed to uncover the biological underpinnings of this variability.

claim: A fraction of many germline de novo mutation datasets are comprised of truly post-zygotic DNMs, rather than mutations that occurred in a single parental gamete.
source: This suggests that a fraction of many germline de novo mutation datasets are comprised of truly post-zygotic DNMs, rather than mutations that occurred in a single parental gamete.
evidence: Inference from observed gonosomal DNM fraction.

claim: The count of gonosomal DNMs may be an underestimate, since the requirement that the second-generation individual be heterozygous precludes the detection of post-zygotic mosaic mutations at very low frequency in blood.
source: We note that our analysis pipeline may erroneously classify some gonosomal and shared germline mosaic DNMs. Namely, our count of gonosomal DNMs may be an underestimate, since our requirement that the second-generation individual be heterozygous precludes the detection of post-zygotic mosaic mutations at very low frequency in blood.

claim: Mosaicism apparently restricted to the germline may, in fact, be present in other somatic cells that were not sampled in this study.
source: Also, blood cells represent only a fraction of the total somatic cell population, and we cannot rule out the possibility that mosaicism apparently restricted to the germline may, in fact, be present in other somatic cells that were not sampled in this study (Biesecker and Spinner, 2013).

claim: A recent study found tentative evidence for a maternal age effect on de novo mutations that arise in the early stages of zygote development.
source: However, a recent study found tentative evidence for a maternal age effect on de novo mutations that arise in the early stages of zygote development (Gao et al., 2019).

claim: The study is likely underpowered to detect a possible maternal age effect on gonosomal DNMs using the numbers of second-generation individuals in the CEPH/Utah dataset.
source: As noted in this previous study, we are likely underpowered to detect a possible maternal age effect using the numbers of second-generation individuals in the CEPH/Utah dataset.

claim: The read tracing and haplotype sharing phasing strategies were highly concordant, with parent-of-origin predictions agreeing at 98.8% (969/980) of all DNMs for which both strategies could be applied.
source: In the second generation, the read tracing and haplotyping sharing phasing strategies were highly concordant, and the parent-of-origin predictions agreed at 98.8% (969/980) of all DNMs for which both strategies could be applied.

claim: The median number of callable autosomal base pairs per sample in the second generation was 2,582,336,232.
source: In the second generation, the median number of callable autosomal base pairs per sample was 2,582,336,232.

claim: The median second-generation germline SNV mutation rate was calculated to be 1.143 × 10−8 per base pair per generation.
source: For each individual, we then divided their count of autosomal de novo mutations by the resulting number of base pairs, and divided the result by two to obtain a diploid human mutation rate per base pair per generation. The median second-generation germline SNV mutation rate was calculated to be 1.143 × 10−8 per base pair per generation.
evidence: Calculated from DNM counts and callable genome fraction.

claim: The missed heterozygote rate (MHR) is estimated to be 0.4%.
source: We estimate the missed heterozygote rate (MHR) to be 0.4%, by dividing the total number of third-generation DNMs with grandparental support by the total number of third-generation DNMs (100/25,075).

claim: In a small number of CEPH/Utah pedigrees, some members of the first-generation (grandparental) generation were not sequenced (6 grandparents in five families).
source: In a small number of CEPH/Utah pedigrees, some members of the first-generation (grandparental) generation were not sequenced (6 grandparents in five families, Supplementary file 1).

claim: The missed heterozygote rate is likely a slight underestimate due to families with unsequenced grandparents.
source: As a result these families are underpowered to detect evidence of third-generation DNM alleles in the first generation, and our MHR is likely a slight underestimate.

claim: Of the 202 de novo mutations called in the four second-generation children of the high-coverage first-generation parents, nine mutations had at least two reads of supporting evidence in the 60X first-generation alignments.
source: Of the 202 de novo mutations called in the four second-generation children of the high-coverage first-generation parents, we find nine mutations with at least two reads of supporting evidence in the 60X first-generation alignments.

claim: The false positive rate for de novo mutation detection is estimated to be approximately 4.5% (9/202).
source: Thus, we estimate our false positive rate for de novo mutation detection to be approximately 4.5% (9/202).
